items.stem: Which term describes the following: “A recurrent, persistent and intrusive thought, urge or image that causes anxiety”?
items.answer: Obsession
items.markingKey: Obsession: a recurrent, persistent and intrusive thought, urge or image that causes anxiety. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Compulsions are maintained by negative reinforcement. Reason (R): Performing a compulsion temporarily reduces anxiety caused by an obsession. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: Relief from anxiety strengthens the compulsion. [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between an obsession and a compulsion.
items.answer: An obsession is an unwanted, intrusive thought, image or urge that causes anxiety (for example fear of contamination); a compulsion is a repetitive behaviour or mental act performed to reduce that anxiety (for example repeated washing).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each with example [2]

items.stem: Mei, from Cairo, spends about three hours a day checking that doors are locked and the cooker is off, and is often late for work because of it. Explain why Mei’s checking is likely to continue.
items.answer: Checking reduces anxiety, so it is negatively reinforced; the obsessional fear is never tested.
items.markingKey: 1 mark negative reinforcement; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: Felix, from Mexico City, spends about three hours a day checking that doors are locked and the cooker is off, and is often late for work because of it. (a) Identify the obsession and the compulsion in this case. (b) Explain why Felix’s checking is likely to continue.
items.answer: (a) Obsession: the intrusive thought that the door is unlocked or the cooker on (fear of harm). Compulsion: repeated checking. (b) Checking reduces anxiety, so it is negatively reinforced; the obsessional fear is never tested.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark negative reinforcement; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: Priya, from Bangkok, spends about three hours a day checking that doors are locked and the cooker is off, and is often late for work because of it. (a) Explain why Priya’s checking is likely to continue. (b) Explain why the Y-BOCS would be useful for Priya’s therapist.
items.answer: (a) Checking reduces anxiety, so it is negatively reinforced; the obsessional fear is never tested. (b) It gives a severity score (for example time occupied and interference) that can be compared before and after treatment to monitor progress.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark negative reinforcement; 1 mark explained [2] (b) 1 mark severity; 1 mark monitoring [2]

items.stem: Which term describes the following: “A repetitive behaviour or mental act that a person feels driven to perform to reduce anxiety”?
items.answer: Compulsion
items.markingKey: Compulsion: a repetitive behaviour or mental act that a person feels driven to perform to reduce anxiety. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “People with OCD always believe their compulsions are sensible.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Most recognise that their obsessions and compulsions are excessive, although insight varies.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Describe how the Y-BOCS measures OCD.
items.answer: A clinician asks about five aspects of obsessions and five of compulsions (time occupied, interference, distress, resistance and control), scoring each 0–4 to give a total from 0 to 40, where higher scores mean more severe OCD.
items.markingKey: 1 mark items/structure; 1 mark scoring; 1 mark interpretation [3]

items.stem: A clinician in Seoul rated Sipho on the Y-BOCS (each item 0–4). Obsession items: 2, 3, 3, 3, 2. Compulsion items: 2, 3, 3, 3, 3. Calculate the total Y-BOCS score.
items.markingKey: 13 (obsessions) + 14 (compulsions) = 27. 1 mark subtotals; 1 mark total [2]

items.stem: Samuel, from Singapore, spends about three hours a day checking that doors are locked and the cooker is off, and is often late for work because of it. (a) Identify the obsession and the compulsion in this case. (b) Explain why Samuel’s checking is likely to continue.
items.answer: (a) Obsession: the intrusive thought that the door is unlocked or the cooker on (fear of harm). Compulsion: repeated checking. (b) Checking reduces anxiety, so it is negatively reinforced; the obsessional fear is never tested.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark negative reinforcement; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: Assess the view that obsessive-compulsive disorder is best explained by biological factors.
items.answer: Arguments for: Family and twin studies suggest a genetic component. SSRIs reduce symptoms, supporting a role for serotonin; brain scans show overactivity in the orbitofrontal cortex–caudate circuit. Arguments against: Cognitive explanations (inflated responsibility, thought–action fusion) explain the content of obsessions. ERP, a behavioural treatment, is highly effective. Biological findings are correlational. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: Which term describes the following: “The belief that having a thought about an action is the same as doing it, or makes it more likely to happen”?
items.answer: Thought–action fusion
items.markingKey: Thought–action fusion: the belief that having a thought about an action is the same as doing it, or makes it more likely to happen. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Brain scans can show differences in people with OCD. Reason (R): PET scans show increased activity in the orbitofrontal cortex and caudate nucleus in many patients. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: This is evidence for a biological explanation. [1]

items.stem: Explain the cognitive explanation of OCD.
items.answer: Everyone has intrusive thoughts, but people with OCD interpret them as meaningful and dangerous (thought–action fusion) and feel responsible for preventing harm (inflated responsibility); this causes anxiety, and compulsions are performed to neutralise it.
items.markingKey: 1 mark normal intrusive thoughts; 1 mark faulty interpretation; 1 mark compulsions neutralise [3]

items.stem: Sofia, a new parent in Singapore, has a sudden image of dropping the baby and now checks the baby many times each night, believing the thought means something terrible will happen. Use the cognitive explanation to explain Sofia’s checking.
items.answer: Sofia interprets a normal intrusive thought as dangerous and feels responsible for preventing harm, so checking is used to reduce anxiety.
items.markingKey: 1 mark interpretation; 1 mark compulsion reduces anxiety [2]

items.stem: “The cognitive explanation of OCD has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including usefulness in your answer.
items.answer: Strength (supporting evidence): People with OCD score higher on measures of inflated responsibility and thought–action fusion than controls. Strength (usefulness): It led to CBT and ERP, which are effective treatments. Weakness (reductionism): It ignores biological evidence such as genetic links and the effectiveness of SSRIs. Weakness (cause and effect): Faulty beliefs may develop as a result of OCD rather than causing it. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: A student writes: “Most people experience intrusive thoughts from time to time.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Research shows intrusive thoughts are common; the difference in OCD is how they are interpreted.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain the biological explanation of OCD.
items.answer: OCD may be partly genetic (it runs in families), may involve low serotonin activity (SSRIs help) and overactivity in a circuit linking the orbitofrontal cortex, caudate nucleus and thalamus, so worry signals are not switched off.
items.markingKey: 1 mark genetics; 1 mark serotonin; 1 mark brain circuit [3]

items.stem: A clinic in Seoul compared Y-BOCS scores (0–40) after 12 weeks for 8 clients with OCD who received exposure and response prevention (ERP) and 8 clients who received relaxation training. Table: Y-BOCS score after 12 weeks — ERP: 14, 9, 15, 15, 18, 16, 18, 17. Relaxation training: 28, 15, 19, 19, 17, 14, 20, 18. What is the mean score for the relaxation training condition, to one decimal place?

items.answer: IV: whether clients received ERP or relaxation training. DV: total score on the Yale–Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (0–40) after 12 weeks.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: IV; 1 mark: DV, operationalised [2]

items.stem: Identify the term for the following: “A therapy in which the client is exposed to obsession triggers and prevented from performing compulsions”.
items.answer: Exposure and response prevention (ERP)
items.markingKey: Exposure and response prevention (ERP): a therapy in which the client is exposed to obsession triggers and prevented from performing compulsions. [1]

items.stem: Describe how exposure and response prevention is used to treat OCD.
items.answer: The client and therapist build a hierarchy of triggers; the client is exposed to each (for example touching a “dirty” object) and prevented from performing the compulsion (washing) until anxiety falls through habituation, moving up the hierarchy.
items.markingKey: 1 mark hierarchy; 1 mark exposure; 1 mark response prevention/habituation [3]

items.stem: Explain one advantage of CBT over SSRIs for OCD.
items.answer: CBT teaches clients to challenge beliefs such as inflated responsibility and to resist compulsions, so gains last after treatment ends, whereas symptoms often return when SSRIs are stopped.
items.markingKey: 1 mark advantage; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: Leila, from Bangkok, has a fear of germs and washes their hands over 50 times a day until the skin bleeds. Explain why ERP might be difficult for Leila.
items.answer: Being prevented from washing will cause intense anxiety at first, so Leila may refuse or drop out.
items.markingKey: 1 mark distress; 1 mark drop-out [2]

items.stem: Ravi, from Lisbon, has a fear of germs and washes their hands over 50 times a day until the skin bleeds. (a) Describe how ERP could be used to help Ravi. (b) Explain why ERP might be difficult for Ravi.
items.answer: (a) Build a hierarchy (for example touching a table, a door handle, a bin lid); expose Ravi to each step and prevent hand-washing for increasing periods until anxiety falls. (b) Being prevented from washing will cause intense anxiety at first, so Ravi may refuse or drop out.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark hierarchy/exposure; 1 mark response prevention [2] (b) 1 mark distress; 1 mark drop-out [2]

items.stem: Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of exposure and response prevention for OCD. Include at least one point about long-term outcome.
items.answer: Strength (long-term outcome): Clients learn skills they can use after therapy, so relapse is lower than when drugs are stopped. Strength (effectiveness): ERP produces large reductions in Y-BOCS scores in many clients, and gains are often maintained. Weakness (individual differences): It works less well for people with purely mental compulsions or with low motivation. Weakness (ethics): Exposure is very distressing, so some clients refuse or drop out of treatment. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.answer: Habituation

items.answer: Build a hierarchy (for example touching a table, a door handle, a bin lid); expose Ana to each step and prevent hand-washing for increasing periods until anxiety falls.
items.markingKey: 1 mark hierarchy/exposure; 1 mark response prevention [2]

items.stem: Yusuf compared Y-BOCS scores after 12 weeks for clients randomly allocated to ERP or relaxation training. Table: Y-BOCS score after 12 weeks — ERP: 16, 8, 16, 15, 7, 16, 12, 40. Relaxation training: 24, 22, 20, 20, 25, 25, 23, 21. (a) Calculate the mean score for each condition. Give your answers to one decimal place. (b) Name the experimental design used in this study and explain one weakness of using this design here.
items.answer: (a) ERP: 16.3; relaxation training: 22.5. (b) Independent measures: different participants take part in each condition. Weakness: participant variables (individual differences between the two groups) may explain the difference in the DV instead of the IV.
items.markingKey: (a) ERP: 130 ÷ 8 = 16.3; relaxation training: 180 ÷ 8 = 22.5. 1 mark for each correct mean [2] (b) 1 mark: correct design; 1 mark: weakness explained in context [2]

items.stem: Evaluate exposure and response prevention for OCD, including a discussion of ethics.
items.answer: Strength (long-term outcome): Clients learn skills they can use after therapy, so relapse is lower than when drugs are stopped. Strength (effectiveness): ERP produces large reductions in Y-BOCS scores in many clients, and gains are often maintained. Weakness (individual differences): It works less well for people with purely mental compulsions or with low motivation. Weakness (ethics): Exposure is very distressing, so some clients refuse or drop out of treatment. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: Which term is defined as the following: “Persistent difficulty discarding possessions, regardless of their value, leading to clutter”?
items.answer: Hoarding disorder
items.markingKey: Hoarding disorder: persistent difficulty discarding possessions, regardless of their value, leading to clutter. [1]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A student writes: “People with OCD always believe their compulsions are sensible.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Describe how the Y-BOCS measures OCD.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Most recognise that their obsessions and compulsions are excessive, although insight varies. (b) A clinician asks about five aspects of obsessions and five of compulsions (time occupied, interference, distress, resistance and control), scoring each 0–4 to give a total from 0 to 40, where higher scores mean more severe OCD.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2] (b) 1 mark items/structure; 1 mark scoring; 1 mark interpretation [3]

items.stem: Outline one strength of the Y-BOCS as a measure of OCD that relates to reliability.
items.answer: It has standardised questions and scoring, and good inter-rater reliability when used by trained clinicians.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant strength linked to reliability; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Leila, from Hanoi, spends about three hours a day checking that doors are locked and the cooker is off, and is often late for work because of it. Explain why Leila’s checking is likely to continue.
items.answer: Checking reduces anxiety, so it is negatively reinforced; the obsessional fear is never tested.
items.markingKey: 1 mark negative reinforcement; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: A clinician in Bogotá rated Lucas on the Y-BOCS (each item 0–4). Obsession items: 1, 2, 2, 2, 2. Compulsion items: 3, 2, 2, 2, 1. (a) Using the bands 0–7 subclinical, 8–15 mild, 16–23 moderate, 24–31 severe and 32–40 extreme, state the severity of OCD. (b) Calculate the percentage of the maximum possible score that the compulsion subscale represents for this client.
items.answer: (a) Moderate (19) (b) 50%
items.markingKey: (a) 19 lies in the moderate band [1] (b) 10 ÷ 20 × 100 = 50%. 1 mark working; 1 mark answer [2]

items.stem: Mei wants to find out whether people with high anxiety check things more often than people with low anxiety. Design an observation to investigate this. Your plan must include: ethical issues, how inter-rater reliability will be checked and the type of observation.
items.answer: Method: an observation. Structured observation with operationalised behavioural categories and time sampling; two observers to check inter-rater reliability; overt or covert as appropriate. Variables: IV: high or low anxiety group; DV: number of checking behaviours in a task. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Lisbon, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: Identify the term for the following: “A frontal brain area that is overactive in many people with OCD and is linked to worry about errors”.
items.answer: Orbitofrontal cortex
items.markingKey: Orbitofrontal cortex: a frontal brain area that is overactive in many people with OCD and is linked to worry about errors. [1]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A student writes: “Most people experience intrusive thoughts from time to time.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain the psychodynamic explanation of OCD.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Research shows intrusive thoughts are common; the difference in OCD is how they are interpreted. (b) Freud suggested OCD arises from conflict between the id and superego, often from harsh toilet training in the anal stage; defence mechanisms such as isolation, undoing and reaction formation produce obsessions and compulsions.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2] (b) 1 mark conflict/anal stage; 1 mark defence mechanisms [2]

items.stem: Explain one weakness of the cognitive explanation of OCD in terms of cause and effect.
items.answer: Faulty beliefs may develop as a result of OCD rather than causing it.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to cause and effect; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: A clinic in Dhaka compared Y-BOCS scores (0–40) after 12 weeks for 7 clients with OCD who received exposure and response prevention (ERP) and 7 clients who received relaxation training. Table: Y-BOCS score after 12 weeks — ERP: 17, 15, 11, 18, 22, 16, 12. Relaxation training: 22, 24, 22, 23, 23, 28, 22. Calculate the mean score for each condition. Give your answers to one decimal place.
items.answer: ERP: 15.9; relaxation training: 23.4.
items.markingKey: ERP: 111 ÷ 7 = 15.9; relaxation training: 164 ÷ 7 = 23.4. 1 mark for each correct mean [2]

items.stem: Samuel, a new parent in Toronto, has a sudden image of dropping the baby and now checks the baby many times each night, believing the thought means something terrible will happen. Use the cognitive explanation to explain Samuel’s checking.
items.answer: Samuel interprets a normal intrusive thought as dangerous and feels responsible for preventing harm, so checking is used to reduce anxiety.
items.markingKey: 1 mark interpretation; 1 mark compulsion reduces anxiety [2]

items.stem: Ravi compared Y-BOCS scores after 12 weeks for clients randomly allocated to ERP or relaxation training. Table: Y-BOCS score after 12 weeks — ERP: 23, 26, 12, 13, 14, 14, 13, 16. Relaxation training: 19, 24, 15, 21, 28, 28, 19, 23. The standard deviation for the ERP condition was 5.21 and for the relaxation training condition was 4.55. Explain what these values show.
items.answer: The ERP condition has the larger standard deviation, so its scores are more spread out around the mean; the other condition’s scores are more consistent.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the condition with the larger spread; 1 mark: explains that a larger SD means scores are more spread around the mean [2]

items.stem: ‘Obsessive-compulsive disorder is best explained by biological factors.’ Evaluate this statement, using evidence from psychology. In your answer, you may refer to cause and effect and reductionism.
items.answer: Arguments for: Family and twin studies suggest a genetic component. SSRIs reduce symptoms, supporting a role for serotonin; brain scans show overactivity in the orbitofrontal cortex–caudate circuit. Arguments against: Cognitive explanations (inflated responsibility, thought–action fusion) explain the content of obsessions. ERP, a behavioural treatment, is highly effective. Biological findings are correlational. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: Define the term ‘habituation’.
items.answer: A decrease in anxiety after repeated or prolonged exposure to a stimulus.

items.answer: (a) Build a hierarchy (for example touching a table, a door handle, a bin lid); expose Jonas to each step and prevent hand-washing for increasing periods until anxiety falls.
